COURT FILE NO.:

07-FL-2179

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

(born July 28, 2007)

)

Society of Ottawa

HEARD:
July 8, 2008 (Ottawa)

DECISION ON A MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT

PURSUANT
TO RULE 16 OF THE
FAMILY LAW RULES

LALONDE J.

[
1
]

The
Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa has presented a motion for a finding that J.S.C. (J.),
born on July 13, 2006 and F.S.C. (F.), born on July 28, 2007 are children in
need of protection pursuant to paragraph 37(2)(b) of the
Child and Family
Services Act
and for an order that the children be made ward of the Crown
without access.

ISSUES

(a)

Is summary judgment appropriate in this case;
has procedural fairness been afforded to the parents?

(b)

Has the Society made out a
prima facie

case that it is in the best interests of the children, J. and F., to be made
wards of the Crown?

(c)

Have the responding parents set out in an
affidavit or other document specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial?

(d)

Have the responding parents shown that: (1) the
relationship between themselves and the children, J. and F., is both meaningful and beneficial to the children; and (2) that ordered
access will not impair the children's future opportunities for adoption?

PAST PARENTING
HISTORY

[
2
]

Counsel for the CAS has consented to my use of her
materials to establish the past parenting history.  The following statements
are well documented and not contradicted by any evidence I received during this
hearing.

[
3
]

The family's file was opened in August 2006, when a
referral was received from Ms. Sue Beatton, the public health nurse
involved with the family. Ms. Beatton reported concerns with respect to
the parents' young age, limited parenting skills and limited support.  This was
the Society's first opening and the file has remained open since this time.

[
4
]

In November 2006, the Ongoing Child Protection Worker
transferred the family's file to the "Family Support Program Team"
for the purpose of providing intensive support to the family.  However, the
file was transferred back to Ongoing Service in March 2007, as the parents did
not engage with the workers from the Family Support Program Team.

[
5
]

From March 2007 to July 2007, K.C. (Ms. C.)
rescheduled, cancelled and failed to show for a number of scheduled
appointments with her ongoing worker.  However, Ms. C. participated in the
Society's Infant Stimulation Program from April 2007 to July 2007.

[
6
]

Also during this time period, the Society received two
police reports regarding verbal altercations between the parents, and Ms. C.
disclosed that D.S.L. (Mr. L.) had been yelling on a regular basis and that she
was afraid that J. would be affected.  The Society workers also documented
concerns with respect to the state/hygiene/safety of the home.

[
7
]

On July 19, 2007, Ms. C. made arrangements to
stay with friends.  On July 28, 2007, Ms. C. gave birth to F. who weighed
5 pounds, 15 ounces.  On August 1, 2007, Ms. C. moved to a shelter for
abused women.  The staff at the shelter reported a number of concerns with
respect to the care Ms. C. was providing for her two young children.

[
8
]

On August 15, 2007, Ms. C. placed the oldest
child, J., in the care of the Society pursuant to a Temporary Care Agreement so
that she could attend her appointments with baby F.  J. was then
returned to his mother on August 27, 2007.

First
Apprehension

[
9
]

On the evening of September 11, 2007, and again on the
morning of September 12, 2007, staff at the women's shelter informed the
Society that the mother had repeatedly stated that she could no longer cope
with the responsibility of caring for her two children.  The children were
subsequently apprehended on September 12, 2007.

[
10
]

The maternal great-grandparents to the children traveled from Mexico to
Canada
(
Toronto
) to
provide care for the children.  The Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan
Toronto completed a Kinship Assessment and the maternal great-grandparents were
approved on the condition that the mother of the children (Ms. C.) would
not reside in the family home.

[
11
]

On November 28, 2007, the children were placed in the care of their
maternal great-grandparents pursuant to a temporary supervision order with
conditions.  They provided care for the children from November 2007 to February
2008.

[
12
]

While the children and mother remained in
Ottawa
(September to October
2007), the Society worker (Ms. Clements) sought to address the children
protection issues with Ms. C.  Ms. C. was not cooperative.  She did
not attend appointments, did not complete urine screens, did not address her
previous ADHD diagnosis as requested by the Society and was not consistent in
attending her access visits.

[
13
]

There were similar concerns with respect to Mr. L.  In October 2007,
the Society worker requested two drug screens, which were not completed by Mr. L.
(Mr. L. stated that he had been using marijuana since 14 years of age to
help him sleep at night.)  Mr. L. attended for two visits before the
children left for
Toronto
.  He was permitted to visit the children in
Toronto
, with
the Society sharing transportation costs, but did not use this opportunity.

[
14
]

Mr. L. indicated that, while the children were in
Toronto
, he
would find a job, find suitable housing, complete anger management, complete a
parenting course and plan for his children.

Second
Apprehension

[
15
]

In January 2008, the Society received a request from the great-grandparents
that the children be placed back into the Society's care as Ms. C. had not
been following through with the Society's expectations, and she had visited her
children on a sporadic basis.

[
16
]

While in Toronto, Ms. C. was to follow through with conditions
outlined by the Society including: a medical follow-up, a mental and emotional
health assessment, parenting courses, random drug screens, attend regularly
scheduled meetings with Society workers, cooperate fully with the Society,
complete an ADHD assessment and attend access at minimum three times weekly
with her children.  Ms. C. did not comply.

[
17
]

On February 6, 2008, the children were transported to
Ottawa
by the
great-grandparents and apprehended.  The children were placed together in a
foster home.  The great-grandparents moved back to
Mexico
.

Events Since
The Second Apprehension

[
18
]

After the children returned from
Toronto
, Ms. C. did not remain in contact with the
Children's Aid Society, but for leaving voice messages, and attending at Court
(March 4, March 31 and April 25).  On March 4, 2008, the worker
scheduled a meeting with Ms. C. (for March 7, 2008) but she did not
attend.  On March 31, 2008, Society counsel advised Ms. C. to call the
worker, but she did not call.

[
19
]

Ms. C.
contacted the Society at the end of April 2008 - two and a half months after
her children were returned to the
Ottawa
jurisdiction.  The Society worker has continued to
review the Society’s expectations with Ms. C., but she had been unable to
demonstrate any level of stability:

a)

She has had difficulty maintaining a stable
residence;

b)

She has advised of her intention to complete
programs at Bethany Hope and/or St. Mary’s and anger management at
Elizabeth Fry but has not followed through with this programming;

c)

She has not submitted any documentation with
respect to her current mental health status as requested;

d)

She has evaded drug screens and provided two
recent screens positive for THC in June 2008;

e)

She has had weekly access visits since May 2008,
but has missed three visits (May 14, June 11, June 25) and most recently
the visit scheduled for the week of June 30
th
.

[
20
]

Further, Ms. C. has also shown that she does not have her children’s
best interests at heart.  While she proposed a kinship plan, wherein her
biological father and stepmother would care for the children, she then
proceeded to provoke and harass her family members until they withdrew their
plan.

[
21
]

The current Society worker, Ms. Debra Webber, met with the father at
court on April 9, 2008 to review his plan of care.  There were a
number of concerns at this time. First, he had recently tested
positive for very high levels of THC.  He advised Ms. Webber that he was
slowing down his use little by little and his next results should be clear.
However, he has subsequently tested at higher levels on April 23, 2008 and May
1, 2008.

[
22
]

Second, the Society has requested a drug assessment but Mr. L. had
not complied nor has he attended for anger management or a medical assessment,
for the purpose of assessing a previous head injury.

[
23
]

Third, Mr. L. has not presented viable living arrangements to the
Society.  He is currently residing with a new partner who is known to the
Children’s Aid Society and has been assessed as a risk to children.  (At the
time of trial Mr. L. informed the Court that he had ceased residing with
this person.)

[
24
]

Most significantly, Mr. L. has missed a significant number of
visits.  Between April 2008 and June 4 2008, nine visits had been
scheduled.  He was late for three, did not show up for two (May 21 and
June 4) and had a visit cancelled because of extreme tardiness (May 14).
Since June 4, 2008, he attended June 11
th
and missed the June 18
th

and June 25
th
visits.

K.C.’ POSITION

[
25
]

Counsel for the mother told
the Court that Ms. C. recently met her biological parents.  The parents, who
had the children in Toronto and gave up caring for the children and returned to
Mexico, were her adoptive parents.  This reunion took place in April 2008 only
and counsel argued that CAS did not take the time to assess this situation.

[
26
]

The mother, through her
counsel, argued that CAS did not provide the services it is mandated to
provide.  No kinship assessment was made on this new situation.  Counsel
claimed that CAS was disrupting a relationship that Ms. C. is trying to
bridge on events that took place 20 years ago.

[
27
]

The CAS, according to the
mother, presented no evidence that her home was unfit.  She lives in an area
where there are other children around.

D.S.L.’S
POSITION

[
28
]

Counsel for the father
pleaded that his client is employed and has the ability to support his
children.  He claimed also that the father has relatives such as his grandmother
that could help him take care of his children.

[
29
]

The father claimed that the
children have been in care less than one year.  He claimed also that the CAS
investigators were all oriented to the mother’s side of the family and that
members of his side of the family were ignored.

[
30
]

Counsel for the father
pointed out that the father followed one parenting program and that it was the
CAS’ responsibility to obtain consent from the father to get such results.  The
father advised the Court that he had terminated his relationship with C.P., an
extremely negative person.

[
31
]

The father acknowledged his
use of marijuana stating that he was trying to diminish his reliance on the
drug.

ANALYSIS AND
DECISION

[
32
]

I find that both J. and F.
are children found to be in need of protection pursuant to paragraph 37(2)(b)
of the
Act
and I order that they be made Crown wards of the Children’s
Aid Society of Ottawa without access for the purpose of adoption.

[
33
]

At the conclusion of this
hearing, I stated in open court that the mother simply does not have what it
takes to look after her children.  It was for this purpose that I reproduced
the CAS’ history of their involvement with the mother and the children.  I
discount all of the mother’s submissions at this hearing.  The mother’s last
affidavit where she apologizes for her behaviour to her biological father, D.B.
and her stepmother, H.L., confirms the affidavit of Jean Isabelle Artelle,
a kinship service worker employed by the Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa
and filed with this Court.  She concludes her affidavit at paragraph 25:

25.  On
June 24
th
, 2008, this worker met with social worker Debra Webber to
inform her the kinship home study on [H.L.] would not be completed due to the
following reasons:

a)  [H.L.]’s
home does not meet Ministry Standards;

b)  [H.L.]’s
financial inability to care for two additional children;

c)  [Ms. C.]’s
unstable relationship with her father, [D.B.] and stepmother, [H.L.];

d)  [Ms. C.]’s
threatening and aggressive behaviour towards [H.L.], including threats made by [Ms. C.]
on June 18
th
, 2008, towards [H.L.];

e)  [H.L.]’s
and [D.B.]’s inability to protect the children from any risks posed by [Ms. C.]

[
34
]

As a result, the least
disruptive disposition for the two children is to grant the order requested so
that the placement parents can adopt the children.

THE LAW

[
35
]

I will now turn to the law
and I adopt the submissions that follow made by counsel for the Children’s Aid
Society of Ottawa.

(a)  Is
summary judgment appropriate in this case; has procedural fairness been
afforded to the parents?

[
36
]

Rule 16 of the
Family Law Rules
governs motions for summary
judgment in child protection proceedings.  Rule 16 states:

16.
(1)
After the respondent has
served an answer or after the time for serving an answer has expired, a party
may make a motion for summary judgment for a final order without a trial on all
or part of any claim made or any defence presented in the case.
O. Reg. 114/99,
r. 16 (1)
.

…

(6)
If there is no genuine issue
requiring a trial of a claim or defence, the court shall make a final order
accordingly.
O. Reg. 114/99, r. 16 (6)
.

…

[
37
]

In determining a motion for summary judgment, the
Child Protection Court
must ensure “procedural fairness” for the parents while giving its
utmost attention to the “... special duty of a child protection court
to place the best interests of the child foremost”.
Justice Lane
spoke
of this balancing of interests in
R.A. v. Jewish Family and Child Service,

[2001] O.J. No. 47
as follows:

20
…
The court cannot be unaware of the fact, as Chapnik J. pointed out, that the
making of an order that a child become a Crown ward without access is a very
serious step having profound effects on child and parents alike.  The court
must ensure that the best interests of the child are adequately addressed on
the available evidence.  Caution is thus called for.  Nevertheless, if the
evidence does not raise a triable issue as to where the best interests of the
child lie, those best interests themselves call for a resolution without the
delay associated with a trial and the resulting prolongation of the state of
uncertainty about the child's future.

[
38
]

PROCEDURAL FAIRNESS
: In the
case before the court, the parents, Ms. C. and Mr. L., have been
afforded procedural fairness.

[
39
]

Both parents are represented by counsel.  Counsel of Record were before
the court at the second appearance of the matter on October 3, 2007.

[
40
]

The parties were aware that the Society planned to proceed by way of
summary judgment motion in May 2008. On May 6, 2008, at the
Child Protection Assignment Court
, Justice Polowin scheduled the summary judgment
motion date for May 29, 2008.  This date was adjourned to further assess a
family plan, which was subsequently withdrawn.

[
41
]

At this time, the Society has fully assessed all plans put forward by the
parents and recorded the results in the affidavits before the Court.

[
42
]

SPECIAL DUTY OF THE COURT
:  In
child protection cases, there is a statutory imperative in place to ensure that
the commencement of permanency planning for children is completed in a
timely fashion. This imperative is found in section 70 of the
Child and
Family Service Act
and allows for children less than six years of age made
to be wards of the Society for a cumulative period of 12 months only.

[
43
]

In this case it is important to note that, while the children have not
yet reached the        12-month mark, they have experienced multiple placements
and instability over their short lives.  J. has resided in the following five
placements: (1) Birth (July 13, 2006) to July 2007 with his mother and father;
(2) July 30, 2007 to August 27, 2007 in the Society's care pursuant to Temporary
Care Agreement; (3) September 12, 2007 in the Society's care pursuant to
apprehension; (4) November 29, 2007 to February 6, 2008 in the grandparents'
care; and (5) February 6, 2008 to present in the Society's care pursuant
to apprehension.

[
44
]

The child F. also experienced multiple placements. She resided with her
mother after birth.  At two months of age, she was placed in the Society's
care.  At four months of age, she was placed with her grandparents. At seven
months of age, she was returned to the Society's care.

(b)
Has
the Society made out a
prima facie
case that it is in the best interests
of the children, J. and F., to be made wards of the Crown?

[
45
]

In order to establish the
prima facie
case, the Applicant Society
must serve an affidavit or other evidence that sets out specific facts showing
that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial.  In other words, the Society
must establish a
prima facie
case.

[
46
]

Specifically, in the present case before the court, the Society must
adduce evidence, which demonstrates that the children are in need of protection
and it is in their best interests to be made wards of the Crown pursuant to the
criteria set out in section 37 of the
Child and Family Services Act
.

[
47
]

Pursuant to Section 57(3) and (4) of the C
hild and Family Services Act
,
the Society must satisfy the Court that the order requested is the least
disruptive alternative and that it is not possible to place the children with a
relative, neighbour or other member of the children’s community or extended
family.

[
48
]

In the case before the Court, the Society has demonstrated through the
evidence of the Society workers that both parents present a risk to the
children and neither parent has been able to present a viable plan of care,
which would address the child protection risks.

[
49
]

Ms. C.’s life is marked by transience and a lack of stability.  She
has not cooperated with the Society or participated in sufficient community
service programs, for the purpose of addressing her mental health, personal
stability or parenting capacity. She is young and her judgment is poor.  She
has proposed two family plans but then proceeded to discourage her family from
assisting her by her harassing behaviour.  She is currently testing positive
for marijuana use and missing significant access visits with her children.

[
50
]

Mr. L. has expressed the best of intentions but not been able to
follow through with addressing any of the children protection concerns.  He has
recently ceased residing with a woman who is known to the Society as a risk to
children.  He is also using marijuana at high levels and missing significant
access visits.

[
51
]

In this case, the father’s
inability to wean himself from his continuous use of marijuana has influenced
my decision.  Despite the fact that the father of the children expressed a belief
in his affidavit of July 4, 2008 that the THC level in his system would
decrease, a sample given by the father and analyzed July 3, 2008 indicates a
positive result for THC above the screening level.  Evidence was tendered by
the Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa after the trial was completed but before
my decision was rendered to the parties.  Because Mr. L. had addressed his
marijuana problem in an affidavit filed with the Court giving the impression
his drug problem was improving, I felt it was fair to accept this evidence
contradicting his statement produced at trial.

(c) Have the responding parents set out in an
affidavit or other document specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial?

[
52
]

Ontario Regulation 114/99,
rule 16(4.1)
states that:

(4.1)
In response to the
affidavit or other evidence served by the party making the motion, the party
responding to the motion may not rest on mere allegations or denials but shall
set out, in an affidavit or other evidence, specific facts showing that there
is a genuine issue for trial. O. Reg. 91/03, s. 5.

[
53
]

In
Transamerica Life Insurance Co. of Canada v. Canada Life Assurance
Co.

(1996),
1996 CanLII 7979 (ON CTGD)
,
28 O.R. (3d) 423 (Ont. Gen. Div.)
affirmed Appeal Court
(Ont. C.A.), the court states:

… It is clearly established that on a motion for summary judgment, a
party is no longer entitled to sit back and rely on the possibility that more
favourable facts may develop at trial. To avoid summary judgment, a party is
required to put its best foot forward. The onus remains on the moving party to
show that there is no genuine issue for trial, but the responding party must
"lead trump or risk losing"…

[
54
]

In
Irving Ungerman Ltd. v. Galanis
(Ont.
C.A.
), Morden A.C.J.O. states:

… it was safe to say that "genuine" means not
spurious and, more specifically, that the words "for trial" assist in
showing meaning for the term. If the evidence on a motion for summary judgment
satisfies the court that there is no issue of fact that requires a trial for
its resolution, the requirements of the rule have been met. It must be clear
that a trial is unnecessary.

[
55
]

In
Aguonie v. Galion Solid Waste Material Inc.
(Ont.
C.A.
), Borins J.A. states:  “An issue of fact must
relate to a material fact.”

[
56
]

In child protection cases, it is important that the court considered the
parents’ evidence cautiously.  It is not sufficient for the responding parents
to simply contradict the evidence adduced by the Social workers.  The parents
must provide evidence to demonstrate a genuine issue for trial, related to a
material fact in the case.  In most cases, the parents must show that the
Society was fundamentally wrong in its assessment of their plan to care for the
child(ren) or that another potentially viable plan has not been assessed.

[
57
]

In the case before the court, the parents have not responded to the
Society’s affidavits in support of the summary judgment motion, in a meaningful
way… meaning that such responses do not raise a triable issue.

[
58
]

It is also important to note that not all issues of credibility will
prevent a court from ruling in favour of a Society’s request.  While, as a
general rule, if there is an issue of credibility a trial is required and
summary judgment should not be granted. The exception is set out in
, supra.
At page 552 it is noted that summary
judgment may be granted where there is no substantial evidence on an issue,
where the evidence that is tendered "is in its nature too incredible to be
accepted by reasonable minds, or that by conceding its truth, it is without
legal probative force."  Morden A.C.J.O. summarizes this in his statement
that, "the proposition that an issue of credibility precludes the granting
of summary judgment applies only when what is said to be an issue of
credibility is a genuine issue of credibility."

(d)
Have
the responding parties shown that: (1) the relationship between them and the
children, J. and F., is both
meaningful and
beneficial to the children; and (2) that ordered
access will not impair the children's future opportunities for adoption?

[
59
]

T
he next issue
is whether the court should order access as between the parents and one or more
of the children. The relevant sections of the
Child and Family Services Act

are sections 59(2) and (2.1).  These sections state:

(2)
Where the court makes an
order that a child be made a ward of the Crown, any order for access made under
this Part with respect to the child is terminated.
2006, c. 5,
s. 17 (2)
.

(2.1)
A court shall not make or
vary an access order made under section 58 with respect to a Crown ward unless
the court is satisfied that,

(a) the relationship between the person and the child is beneficial and
meaningful to the child; and

(b) the ordered access will not impair the child's future opportunities
for adoption.
2006, c. 5, s. 17 (2)
.

[
60
]

Section 63.1 states that:

63.1
Where a child is made a
Crown ward, the society shall make all reasonable efforts to assist the child
to develop a positive, secure and enduring relationship within a family through
one of the following:

1. An adoption.

2. A custody order under subsection 65.2 (1).

…

[
61
]

In the case before the court, the parents have not led any evidence with
respect to access issues.

[
62
]

As the children are young, without any serious medical or psychological
issues, the legislation mandates that they be given the opportunity of a
permanent placement with a family through adoption.

[
63
]

The father attempted to make a case that family members would come to his
help.  However, none of the family members were present in court for this
hearing and none have presented materials. I believe that CAS would have been
happy to investigate any family member coming forward in the last six months
with a plan of care but no family members did.  Debra Webber, a child
protection worker with the Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa, filed an affidavit
stating that she had repeated conversations with Mr. L. on his need to
prepare a plan of care and that no such plan was prepared.  She also states
that if Mr. L. has been working, he has not been working for very long as
he told her he was on social assistance on April 9, 2008.

[
64
]

In her July 7, 2008
Ms Webber addresses the father’s statement that family members would help
him with the children. Mr. L. had indicated to Ms. Webber, as far
back as April 2008, that his sister would help.  His sister, with whom he
was supposed to live, never came to be interviewed by CAS and Mr. L. moved
in with his girlfriend.

[
65
]

In May 2008, Mr. L.
indicated to Ms. Webber that his father would attend with him for visits.
This never materialized and Mr. L.’s father and stepmother knew who
Ms. Webber was, as she had spoken to them often, as Mr. L.
resided with them for some time.

[
66
]

For the above reasons, I
grant Crown wardship to the Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa for J. and F. without
access for the purposes of adoption.

[
67
]

These children are entitled
to permanency planning.  Permanency planning, in this case, means allowing the
children to be adopted into a home where all their needs can be met by their
new adoptive parents.  Given J. and F.’s young age and their undisputed ability
likely to form emotional bonds with their adoptive parents, they would enjoy a
greater and more secure form of permanency by being adopted, especially since
the foster parents have indicated a willingness to adopt J. and F.  Adoption is
inconsistent with continued access.

________________________________

Mr.
Justice Paul F. Lalonde

Released:
July
21, 2008

COURT FILE NO.:
07-FL-2179

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

, R.S.O. 1990

AND
IN THE MATTER OF J.S.C. (born July 13, 2006 and F.S.C. (born July 28,
2007)

B E T W E E N:

THE CHILDREN’S AID SOCIETY OF OTTAWA

Applicant

– and –

K.C. (mother) and D.S.L. (father)

Respondents

DECISION ON A MOTION

FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT

PURSUANT TO RULE 16 OF
